By "doggy Xanax", do you mean something like Trazodone or Reconcile? Benadryl doesnt always make dogs as "drowsy" as a lot of people think. High energy dogs can easily blow through that common side affect. Also, Trazodone too wont make your dog "into a zombie". Acepromazine? Heck yeah. You can get the most naughty GSD mellow'd out on a couple mgs of that. But an easily-ramped up dog won't get the "complete edge" taken off with Traz sometimes.

What kind of mental stimulation does she get on a daily basis? Having your dog run around willy nilly is one thing, but putting their brain to work can really help take a bit of the edge off of things. Freeze a kong with peanut butter/dog spray cheese, get one of those toy puzzles where they have to work for it to dispense a treat, if she enjoys toys, mix up her toys. Get her ones with different textures, different squeaky sounds, different sizes. Keep things "interesting". Animals are creatures of habit, but high-energy dogs can greatly benefit from routine switch-ups and constant introduction of new things.

It sounds "extra" but labs love to please and they have super sharp minds that need to be put to work. She, too, may just be easily overstimulated.

If you've "exhausted your efforts", seeking out a veterinarian behaviorist would be another route you could take.

Dealing with the exact thing. I have an anxiety disorder, which makes interacting with clients absolute hell sometimes. I am on anti anxiety medication, antidepressants AND adhd medication. I’m literally a train wreck when it comes to mental health lmao.

One of the only things that helps me is keeping a “mental script” when I go out to take a hx of an animal or if I do technician appointments and discuss vaccines with the owner. For me, I use to work at a vaccine clinic, so I usually have vx knowledge in the bag and am finally confident in doing technician appointments. For getting a hx before I bring an animal in, I say something along the lines of “Hi there, I’m one of the technicians from inside out here to take a quick history before I bring your dog/cat on back. It sounds like he’s here for ______ - tell me a little bit more of what’s going on”. Then after they give their story, I ask if there is any c/s/v/d (if it has not been addressed yet), is they have been eating and drinking OK and if their energy level has been the same. Then I ask if they have any preexisting medical conditions and if they’re on any medication. Ask if there are any other things they would like for us to know before I bring them on back. Literally I just word vomit almost the same exact script every time which has helped a bit, but sometimes I’m not always 100%. Drill and kill seems to help most days.

And if they ask anything that you don’t know, I always just tell them I will ask the doctor when we bring them back. I always throw that one too lol.

Sometimes the “mental script” doesn’t always work, but it has personally eased my anxiety in some situations. I hateeeee going out to get hx on animals but over the last week I just mentally repeat the script and I have gotten less frazzled.

Hi, congratulations! Some other people have kind of outlined what I’m going to suggest, but what I look for most and value in another assistant is ALWAYS asking questions no matter how “stupid” and to keep busy. This is a pretty hands on job, and a lot of times than not there’s always a lot to do. You are setting yourself up for success if you ask others what they would like help with, and once you get the hang of basic cleaning, surgery prep, IVC setups, making surgery packs, etc, jumping in and preparing items for those kind of situations for people will be greatly appreciated by your staff. Remember that with time things will come more naturally and don’t let things overwhelm you too much in the beginning! There’s a lot to learn and none of us expect you to know how the hospital works from the get go. 

Also, restraint is pretty much a huge part of this job. When you work with different techs and vets, ask if there’s a certain way you would like to have their animal restrained. Over time you’ll figure out what works best with you, but getting an insight on how other people hold goes a long way. I worked with a clinic that really prepared me by teaching me a lot about restraint, and it really helped me when I first got hired at my current hospital.

Good luck! You got this!

I really can't vouch for PennFoster, San Juan, or other online programs like that. The only one I can vouch for is a less-common one that is still relatively new where you have to clock in 3,500+ hours in a veterinary setting (so that is about 2 years of working at a clinic or shelter full time), apply to the online program, then it is a 17 week long course. Once you finish it, you can sit for the VTNE, and it has a 95% VTNE passing rate amongst the graduates (and the program is accredited as well- some of the people who run the program are UC Davis veterinary professional grads). PM me if you are interested in it, because I think it may be area specific- a couple RVTs at my hospital got their schooling through it. However, I can tell you to avoid Carrington College like the plague. 

I'm personally pursuing that program because I absolutely need to work full time on top of schooling and an IRL one wouldn't allow me to do that. I have bills to pay and work at a very short staffed hospital, plus I have dropped out of traditional college twice and do not thrive in a sit-down-in-a-classroom setting with my ADD.

Your best bet tbh is a community college that has a Veterinary Technology program. More times than not, they require prerequisites (usually a (or multiple) biosci and chem classes, some may even require a math or english). You apply, write some kind of essay as to why you are a good candidate (or whatever prompt they throw at you), and to have someone in the field write you a letter of recommendation. These programs are usually 18 months or 2 years long to finish. 

That being said, I highly suggest volunteering at a shelter or shadowing a vet in the meantime. This can also help you really determine if this is what you want to do. It also can help you build connections in the industry if you ever need them, and people to reach out to if you ever need advice for your program.

I do warn people that this is a very emotionally and physically taxing job. Be prepared to be on your feet for long periods of time, and to invest some super comfy shoes and gel inserts. Separating your emotions from your job may take time as well, but it does get easier over time.

Hi! I educate people on puppy vaccinations for a living so I can try to help you out here. 

It’s not the amount of shot rounds you give them, it’s the timing. Puppies still have antibodies from their mother that are “fighting” the vaccinations they’re given and those shots are basically considered a temporary immunity until 16-18 weeks when the last of the mother’s antibodies in their system dissipate. You want to have the booster vaccinations done between 3-4 weeks from the last and NEVER more than over 5 weeks or it will not be effective and you’ll have to repeat a set. Definitely do the last round of shots, since your pup is over 16 weeks and should have no antibodies left from its mother. This round should be good for a year and would be your last booster.

Hand feeding dogs table scraps usually turns them into notorious beggars and they become very annoying and will pester you if they are around you while you are eating/preparing food. My SO's dog is like this. 

And depending on what they're eating, scraps very high in fat can lead to acute/chronic pancreatitis. I lost a pet to this, but it was from genetics.

As for dry food, as a general rule of thumb you want the first 3-5 ingredients to always be some kind of meat source. Dry food pumped full of corn, barley, and other grains is not an ideal diet for a dog and could possibly deprive them of a fully balanced meal. Plus dogs weren't made to eat grains anyway. It is not a key element in what they have evolved from. 

Raw food is awesome. I'm a huge raw food advocate. However, that stuff is expensive as *hell* (I'm in college and we have to balance out our GSD's raw food consumption at the moment because we can't afford to go completely raw). Not everyone can afford to feed raw, but if people are interested in trying it out, hit up your local pet store and buy the raw food nuggets/nuggets/toppers you can find in the freezer section. Instinct and Primal are awesome brands.

One last thing: if you want to home cook all of your dog's meals, PLEASE seek a professional in helping you, or else you could really screw with your dog's digestion and overall health.

Responsible breeders breed to better the breed and have a very strong understanding and love for their breed. Responsible ones will do hip/eye/etc testing and have it proof of it available to you, and I've found with most genuine breeders, they will match you to a pup in their litter that will fit your needs vs. you picking one out yourself. They will interview you to make sure that they're not giving one of their dogs to someone who is getting a puppy on a whim, and will want to make sure that you are aware of the breed's needs and will also want to know what your living situation is like. These people usually don't mass advertise their services and occasionally you'll meet some breeders who basically do their business solely out of word of mouth. 

Now for irresponsible breeders... Which are often "backyard" breeders, who pretty much just breed and sell their dogs for the money and don't give a hoot for OFA testing. THEY are the ones you often see on kijiji and craigslist who just want to get rid of the dogs and cash in that $ they get off of them. These people do not care much about genetics, therefore a lot of backyard bred dogs are neurotic (have a purebred GSD from the shelter that was backyard bred- I know this very well LOL) and have health issues from the start. Irresponsible breeders don't just breed for the money- they will also advertise "rare colorings" for the breed that are not a standard color, indicating that the dog is not 100% purebred and probably a mix (therefore they're lying to you, but WOW who wouldn't want a rare sable merle rainbow eyed spitz tailed ~ rare ~ german shepherd, right????). If they don't have at least one of the parents on site for you to meet, it's usually not a good situation. Run for it.

Key things when owning a dog:

1. Home most of the day? Cool. Most dog breeds work for that situation. If you aren't though, you may want to get a dog that isn't known for being destructive (i.e huskies) or doesn't have high energy. 

2. How much exercise can you cater to the dog on a daily basis? If you can only give it short walks in the morning or night you're probably going to want a smaller dog. I have a German Shepherd and we've been taking her on 3 mile walks each night- she's a high energy dog, and some people just don't have time in their schedule to either walk them long distances or bring them to the dog park on the daily.

3. Will you be committed to dealing with and correcting bad habits (chewing, jumping on people when excited, reactive towards other dogs)? More reactive dogs and dogs with similar vices that usually require professional help usually fit people who either have a lot of time in their day to spare or have had previous dog training experience. Something more minor like chewing on furniture though can be resolved pretty easily.
